When concerns about an issuer's creditworthiness increase, demand for protection typically rises, widening CDS spreads.
Payouts are not a given. When Swiss lender Credit Suisse collapsed and was taken over by rival UBS in 2023, the EMEA Credit Derivatives Determinations Committee (CDDC) ruled that event would not trigger a CDS payout.
IF IT'S INSURANCE, WHAT'S THE PROBLEM?
CDS provide a hedge for bondholders. But rising perceived risk pushes up the cost of protection, which can prompt investors to sell bonds and raise borrowing costs for issuers.
That can amplify concerns about creditworthiness and potentially create a self-reinforcing cycle.

Explainer-Why are credit default swaps unnerving AI investors?

LONDON, Oct 15 : The cost of insuring against the risk of potential US tech defaults has hit record levels in the latest sign of credit stress building in the so-called AI trade, especially for data centres dependent on future revenue.
Although shares in companies driving the AI boom are still among the biggest gainers on global equity markets this year, many have fallen sharply in the past few weeks, as investors reassess the cost of capital against a backdrop of rising interest rates and inflation.
There are also doubts among some investors and analysts about when, and in some cases, if, the billions of dollars pouring into data centres, computer power and other infrastructure will pay off.
Demand for AI-linked credit default swaps (CDS), a form of insurance against default that gained prominence during the 2008 financial crisis, meanwhile has surged, even for heavyweights like Apple, Amazon and Microsoft.

For some of their more heavily indebted competitors, suppliers and customers the cost of CDS has risen even faster.
WHAT IS A CDS?
A derivative that provides protection against the risk that a bond issuer, whether a company or government, fails to meet its debt obligations.
Bond investors expect to receive interest payments and repayment of principal when a bond matures, but they bear the risk that those payments may not be made.
Buying CDS helps investors hedge that risk by effectively providing insurance against a default or other credit event. If the value of a bond drops for any reason, an investor might add to their CDS holdings to help offset that, for example.
None of the companies whose CDS have risen recently have defaulted on their obligations or signalled that they may do so.
IS THIS A BIG MARKET?
The market for single-name CDS, which cover the bonds of a single issuer, is worth about $9 trillion, the International Swaps and Derivatives Association (ISDA) said.
That is a small portion of global bond markets, which have more than $150 trillion of debt securities outstanding, Bank for International Settlements data shows.
The biggest CDS market is for government debt.
Average daily CDS trading across the market was $16 billion in the second quarter, up from $13 billion a year earlier, the most recent data from the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation shows. Saudi Arabia is the most actively traded.
But average daily trades, even for large companies, can sometimes be in the single digits, meaning small transactions can have an outsized impact on prices.
WHO BUYS CDS?
Bond investors typically buy CDS through an intermediary, often an investment bank, which then finds a financial firm to issue an insurance policy on the bonds. These are "over-the-counter" deals that do not go through a central clearing house.
Hedge funds also participate in the market, selling CDS to investors seeking to hedge exposure.
The buyer pays a fee, called a premium, at regular intervals to the seller, which assumes the risk of a credit event.
CDS are quoted as a credit spread, which is the number of basis points (bps) that the seller of the derivative charges the buyer for providing protection. The higher the perceived risk of a credit event, the wider the spread.
A CDS quoted at 100 bps costs $1 annually to insure every $100 of debt.
WHAT'S GOING ON WITH TECH CDS?
CDS for CoreWeave, a heavily indebted data centre operator at the eye of the current storm, have risen above 1,000 bps, S&P Global Market Intelligence data show.
They suggest a roughly 63 per cent chance of a default over the next five years, up from around 30 per cent a year ago.
Tech CDS moves reflect investor concern over how quickly massive investments in AI will translate into profits, and whether heavily indebted companies can generate returns fast enough to service mounting interest costs.
Oracle has seen its CDS trade at nearly 300 bps, well above those of other AI-linked companies.
Nvidia CDS have also risen sharply in recent weeks to around 90 bps, Meta CDS are trading around 104 bps.
By comparison, an index of investment-grade CDS is trading around 60 bps.
WHAT TRIGGERS A CDS PAYOUT?
A CDS pays out following a credit event, which can include a bankruptcy or a failure by an issuer to make bond payments.
When concerns about an issuer's creditworthiness increase, demand for protection typically rises, widening CDS spreads.
Payouts are not a given. When Swiss lender Credit Suisse collapsed and was taken over by rival UBS in 2023, the EMEA Credit Derivatives Determinations Committee (CDDC) ruled that event would not trigger a CDS payout.
IF IT'S INSURANCE, WHAT'S THE PROBLEM?
CDS provide a hedge for bondholders. But rising perceived risk pushes up the cost of protection, which can prompt investors to sell bonds and raise borrowing costs for issuers.
That can amplify concerns about creditworthiness and potentially create a self-reinforcing cycle.

items.title: Enrique y su esposa Meghan hacen su primera aparición conjunta desde su regreso al Reino Unido
items.author: Hannah McKay, Vitalii Yalahuzian
items.creator: Hannah McKay, Vitalii Yalahuzian
items.summary: El príncipe Enrique y su esposa Meghan aparecieron juntos en público el jueves por primera vez desde que regresaron por sorpresa a Gran Bretaña, volviendo a la ciudad donde realizaron su primer compromiso oficial conjunto hace nueve años.
items.body:
El príncipe Enrique y su esposa Meghan aparecieron juntos en público el jueves por primera vez desde que regresaron por sorpresa a Gran Bretaña, volviendo a la ciudad donde realizaron su primer compromiso oficial conjunto hace nueve años.
Harry, el hijo menor del rey Carlos, y Meghan sorprendieron al monarca y al resto de la familia real cuando se trasladaron de California a Inglaterra hace dos meses con sus hijos, el príncipe Archie, de 7 años, y la princesa Lilibet, de 5.
En su primera aparición pública conjunta desde entonces, la pareja regresó a Nottingham, en el centro de Inglaterra, ciudad que ya visitaron en 2017, poco después de que se anunciara su boda.
Comenzaron visitando un estudio de grabación gestionado por una organización benéfica juvenil y comunitaria que ha recibido el apoyo de una donación de 1,1 millones de libras (1,46 millones de dólares) anunciada por Enrique el año pasado.
Más tarde tenían previsto visitar una organización benéfica que lucha contra la pobreza alimentaria, dirigida por un grupo llamado Himmah, a la que Meghan donó 10.000 libras procedentes de las ventas de un libro de cocina publicado para recaudar fondos tras el incendio de la Torre Grenfell de Londres.
El programa de actividades concluye con una visita a otra organización benéfica a la que la pareja ha prestado su apoyo, dedicada a los jóvenes y vinculada a su anterior visita en 2017.
DIVISIÓN EN LA OPINIÓN PÚBLICA Harry y Meghan, el duque y la duquesa de Sussex, se han convertido en figuras profundamente polarizantes desde que renunciaron a sus obligaciones reales para mudarse a California en 2020, y han vertido críticas mordaces tanto contra la familia del príncipe como contra la propia institución real.
Las encuestas de opinión muestran que la mayoría de los británicos tiene una opinión negativa de ellos, aunque los jóvenes se muestran mucho más comprensivos.
En su visita a Nottingham hace nueve años, fueron recibidos por una gran multitud que agitaba banderas y les aclamaba. La visita del jueves fue un acto mucho más discreto, pero la pareja charló con unos 100 escolares emocionados y simpatizantes, a los que se unieron numerosos medios de comunicación.
Meghan se mostró emocionada cuando una mujer le entregó un gran ramo de flores y le dio un abrazo.
"Solo queríamos apoyarte", le dijo otra simpatizante. "Queríamos estar aquí… lo entendemos, queríamos que supieras que te hemos mostrado mucho cariño".
Cuando Enrique hizo su primera aparición pública en solitario desde su traslado, declaró que era "bueno estar de vuelta en suelo británico", pero su regreso no ha estado exento de dificultades.
La ubicación de su nuevo hogar se ha mantenido en secreto por motivos de seguridad y no viven en una residencia real.
Tuvieron que cambiar a sus hijos de colegio poco después de que comenzara el curso por motivos de seguridad, y el portavoz de la pareja también condenó las acciones de "ciertos paparazzi europeos" que se entrometían en su intimidad.

items.title: Deutscher Reederverband alarmiert - Bessere Sicherung von Seewegen
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Angesichts der wachsenden Bedrohungen für die Handelsschifffahrt fordern Deutschlands Reeder von der Politik mehr Einsatz zur Sicherung der Seewege. "Wir sind an einem Punkt angelangt, an dem die gleichzeitige Eskalation auf mehreren zentralen Seewegen die regelbasierte Ordnung auf See insgesamt gefährdet. Angriffe auf zivile Schiffe und die Blockade freier Durchfahrten dürfen nicht zur Normalität werden", erklärte der Hauptgeschäftsführer des Verbands Deutscher Reeder (VDR), Martin Kröger, am Donnerstag. "Die Staatengemeinschaft muss dieser Entwicklung gemeinsam entgegenwirken - mit Diplomatie, internationaler Zusammenarbeit und wirksamem Schutz für Handelsschiffe und ihre Besatzungen."
items.body:
Angesichts der wachsenden Bedrohungen für die Handelsschifffahrt fordern Deutschlands Reeder von der Politik mehr Einsatz zur Sicherung der Seewege. "Wir sind an einem Punkt angelangt, an dem die gleichzeitige Eskalation auf mehreren zentralen Seewegen die regelbasierte Ordnung auf See insgesamt gefährdet. Angriffe auf zivile Schiffe und die Blockade freier Durchfahrten dürfen nicht zur Normalität werden", erklärte der Hauptgeschäftsführer des Verbands Deutscher Reeder (VDR), Martin Kröger, am Donnerstag. "Die Staatengemeinschaft muss dieser Entwicklung gemeinsam entgegenwirken - mit Diplomatie, internationaler Zusammenarbeit und wirksamem Schutz für Handelsschiffe und ihre Besatzungen."
Wie nah die Gewalt inzwischen an Europa heranreiche, zeigten die jüngsten Angriffe auf Handelsschiffe im Schwarzen Meer. Der VDR bezog sich darauf, dass vor der Küste Bulgariens Frachtschiffe von Drohnen getroffen worden waren und eines der Schiffe sank. Inzwischen wurden nach Angaben Rumäniens auch vor dessen Küste zwei Schiffe von Drohnen getroffen. Sowohl Bulgarien als auch Rumänien sind Nato- und EU-Länder.
Der VDR verwies zudem auf wiederholte Angriffe im Persischen Golf und rund um die Straße von Hormus sowie auf weiterhin drohende Attacken von Huthi-Rebellen im Roten Meer. "Die Folgen treffen unsere auf Rohstoffimporte angewiesene Wirtschaft ebenso wie uns Verbraucher beim Heizen, im Supermarkt oder an der Tankstelle. Sichere Seewege sind Grundlage unseres Wohlstandes und einer bezahlbaren Versorgung", sagte Kröger. Risiken für wichtige Handelsverbindungen gebe es auch durch Spannungen um Taiwan. "Vor der deutschen Haustür in der Ostsee erschweren zudem Störungen und Manipulationen von Satellitennavigationssignalen wie GPS die sichere Navigation."
Trotz der angespannten Lage bleibe die Seeschifffahrt verlässlich, erklärte der Branchenverband. Reedereien und Besatzungen hielten die Versorgung mit angepassten Routen und langen Umwegen aufrecht. "Dass Waren weiterhin ankommen, darf nicht darüber hinwegtäuschen, wie gefährdet ihre Lieferwege inzwischen sind. Den höchsten Preis zahlen Seeleute, die bei Angriffen verletzt oder getötet werden", betonte Kröger.
"Seewege schützen sich nicht von allein. Die Menschen, die unsere Versorgung sichern, brauchen selbst Sicherheit." Der VDR appelliere deshalb an die Bundesregierung und Partner, die diplomatischen Bemühungen zur Beendigung der Angriffe zu verstärken, freie Durchfahrten zu sichern und Schutzmaßnahmen zu koordinieren. Dazu gehören auch ausreichend ausgestattete Marinen und Schutzmissionen wie Aspides.

• The agreements cover up to 16 power-island units of 720 megawatts each, alongside associated transformer equipment

items.title: CoreWeave shares, bonds slide further as AI debt fears mount
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: AI cloud firm CoreWeave's shares and bonds slumped further on Thursday despite CEO assurances about its strong deal backlog, in one of the deepest crises of investor confidence yet in an AI build-out increasingly fueled by borrowing.
items.body:
AI cloud firm CoreWeave's (CRWV.O) shares and bonds slumped further on Thursday despite CEO assurances about its strong deal backlog, in one of the deepest crises of investor confidence yet in an AI build-out increasingly fueled by borrowing.
The company's stock fell 6% in premarket trading after a more than 15% drop on Wednesday, among the biggest decliners in a global tech stocks rout. The yield on its April-issued bonds due 2031 surged past 16%, above the level that typically signals distress, drawing a "yikes" from Elon Musk on social media.
Loss-making CoreWeave, which has around $50 billion in debt, has in recent days become the focus of growing doubts about whether the tech industry can sustain a data center boom that is saddling newer cloud firms with heavy borrowing and straining cash flow even at giants such as Google-owner Alphabet.
The cost of insuring the Nvidia-backed company's debt against default has climbed to around 1,000 basis points, a level that implies a nearly 63% chance the company defaults within five years, up from about 30% a year ago.
CoreWeave leads a group of newer cloud providers known as neoclouds, which rent out computing power from tight in supply and costly Nvidia processors to meet the tech industry's soaring demand, often leaning on borrowing to fund the chip purchases.
Critics say that leaves such firms exposed to any cooling in AI demand, while the chips lose value as newer generations arrive, forcing another round of heavy spending to replace them.
CoreWeave, which in August raised its annual capital spending forecast by $4 billion to between $35 billion and $39 billion, is expected to post revenue of nearly $13 billion this year and a loss of $2.13 billion, according to analysts' estimates.
Growing worries about the build-out, on which US tech giants are expected to spend more than $700 billion this year, have in recent days rippled through the stocks that have been the market's biggest winners since ChatGPT's November 2022 launch.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, a closely watched gauge of semiconductor stocks, has erased over $1.6 trillion in market value in an 11.6% slide over the past six sessions. The tech-heavy Nasdaq has declined more than 3% in the period.
On Thursday, tech shares fell across Asia, Europe and the US, dragging broader markets lower on fears that high and rising interest rates could bring a reckoning for the sector.
CoreWeave's neocloud rivals such as Nebius (NBIS.O) , Applied Digital (APLD.O) and Iren (IREN.O) fell between 3.2% and 5%.
'UNLIMITED' POOLS OF CAPITAL The CoreWeave sell-off came as its co-founder Brannin McBee told the Financial Times the company was seeking an investment-grade rating that would open the door to "unlimited" capital.
On the same day, research firm Gartner said that about 80% of neoclouds could shut down by 2030, and that more than $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could face impairment if AI providers keep up their current pace of investment.
"In 2026, AI providers are expected to spend nearly $1 trillion on AI infrastructure, and are forecast to invest an additional $6 trillion between 2027 and 2030,” said Will Sommer, analyst at Gartner.
"However, our research indicates enterprise and consumer AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures during this period.”

The company's stock fell 6 per cent in premarket trading after a more than 15 per cent drop on Wednesday, among the biggest decliners in a global tech stocks rout. The yield on its April-issued bonds due 2031 surged past 16 per cent, above the level that typically signals distress, drawing a "yikes" from Elon Musk on social media.

The cost of insuring the Nvidia-backed company's debt against default has climbed to around 1,000 basis points, a level that implies a nearly 63 per cent chance the company defaults within five years, up from about 30 per cent a year ago.
CoreWeave leads a group of newer cloud providers known as neoclouds, which rent out computing power from tight in supply and costly Nvidia processors to meet the tech industry's soaring demand, often leaning on borrowing to fund the chip purchases.
Critics say that leaves such firms exposed to any cooling in AI demand, while the chips lose value as newer generations arrive, forcing another round of heavy spending to replace them.
CoreWeave, which in August raised its annual capital spending forecast by $4 billion to between $35 billion and $39 billion, is expected to post revenue of nearly $13 billion this year and a loss of $2.13 billion, according to analysts' estimates.
Growing worries about the build-out, on which US tech giants are expected to spend more than $700 billion this year, have in recent days rippled through the stocks that have been the market's biggest winners since ChatGPT's November 2022 launch.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, a closely watched gauge of semiconductor stocks, has erased over $1.6 trillion in market value in an 11.6 per cent slide over the past six sessions. The tech-heavy Nasdaq has declined more than 3 per cent in the period.
On Thursday, tech shares fell across Asia, Europe and the US, dragging broader markets lower on fears that high and rising interest rates could bring a reckoning for the sector.
CoreWeave's neocloud rivals such as Nebius, Applied Digital and Iren fell between 3.2 per cent and 5 per cent.
'UNLIMITED' POOLS OF CAPITAL
The CoreWeave sell-off came as its co-founder Brannin McBee told the Financial Times the company was seeking an investment-grade rating that would open the door to "unlimited" capital.
On the same day, research firm Gartner said that about 80 per cent of neoclouds could shut down by 2030, and that more than $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could face impairment if AI providers keep up their current pace of investment.
"In 2026, AI providers are expected to spend nearly $1 trillion on AI infrastructure, and are forecast to invest an additional $6 trillion between 2027 and 2030,” said Will Sommer, analyst at Gartner.
"However, our research indicates enterprise and consumer AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures during this period.”
CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator pushed back on the concerns in an internal memo on Wednesday seen by Reuters, telling employees the company's deal backlog more than covers its debt obligations and that markets can sometimes "misunderstand and act irrationally."

items.title: パキスタンで学校の屋根崩落、生徒ら33人死亡　増築で過荷重か
items.author: ロイター
items.creator: ロイター
items.summary: [イスラマバード １５日 ロイター] -
items.body:
[イスラマバード １５日 ロイター] - パキスタン北西部ペシャワルで１５日午前、授業中だった学校の屋根が崩落し、生徒少なくとも３２人と教員１人が死亡した。警察と救助当局が明らかにした。

救助隊は私立学校「アルハイル教育センター」のがれきの中から子どもたちを助け出す作業を数時間にわたり続けた。校舎の外には、安否を案じる保護者や親族が詰めかけた。救助当局によると、死亡した生徒の大半は１３歳未満で、少なくとも４５人が重軽傷を負った。

上階の屋根が下の教室にいた児童・生徒の上に崩れ落ち、校舎の２つの階が押しつぶされたという。

ペシャワルの警察署長は「建物の構造が脆弱だった。その上に増築され屋根に過大な荷重がかかり崩落につながった」と指摘。学校の所有者を逮捕し、捜査を開始したと明らかにした。

シャリフ首相は犠牲者の家族に哀悼の意を表した。

items.title: Fintech startup Ramp hits $60 billion valuation after $1.85 billion funding round
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Financial technology startup Ramp said on Thursday it had raised $1.85 billion in a primary financing round led by Dragoneer Investment Group, valuing the company at $60 billion, as the company expands its artificial intelligence offerings.
items.body:
Financial technology startup Ramp said on Thursday it had raised $1.85 billion in a primary financing round led by Dragoneer Investment Group, valuing the company at $60 billion, as the company expands its artificial intelligence offerings.
The funding underscores growing investor interest in financial automation, as corporate software companies add artificial intelligence to expense management, procurement and treasury functions once dominated by legacy enterprise players.
Ramp's valuation marks a rise from [USN:L4N42C0YI TEXT:"$44 billion in June"], when it raised $750 million in a funding round.
The New York-based company, which provides corporate cards and expense management software, said it generates more than $2 billion in annualized revenue and has positive cash flow.
Founded in 2019, Ramp serves more than 85,000 companies, which collectively account for more than $275 billion in annualized purchase volume, up 175% from a year earlier.
The company is also expanding into artificial intelligence tools, including software to monitor AI spending and optimize the cost of running AI models.
The latest round was co-led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Sands Capital and Avenir Growth. Other investors included Fidelity Management & Research Company, T. Rowe Price, GIC and Coatue, the company said.
Ramp said it has raised approximately $5 billion in total equity financing, including the latest round.

FAST

BENGALURU, Oct 15 : The ATP outlined plans on Thursday to substantially boost its bonus pool and reshape its rankings and calendar from 2028 under a package projected to lift player compensation to $350 million while seeking to ease growing concerns over player workload.
The men's and women's tours have faced mounting criticism over their demanding 11-month seasons, while players have pushed for a greater share of revenue and better welfare benefits amid wider concerns about the demands and costs of competing.
Under proposals presented by ATP Chairman Andrea Gaudenzi, the men's tour's bonus pool would rise from $21.5 million to $50 million, with another $25 million for year-end top-250 players and $30 million annually for pensions covering 300 players.
"Tennis is in a strong position today," Gaudenzi wrote in an open letter released on Thursday.

"Our events continue to grow, fans are engaging with the sport in more ways than ever and player earnings have reached record levels. To stay strong, the sport has to keep evolving.
"We have a responsibility to strengthen competition, better align incentives and extend support to more players, helping them to address the costs of competing on the tour."
CLEARER STRUCTURE FOR TOUR
Subject to further consultation and approval, the ATP's central player compensation would exceed $100 million from 2028, with prize money and profit-sharing taking total player compensation to a projected $350 million before any Grand Slam prize money is taken into account.
The ATP also plans to give results at its biggest events greater rankings weight, reducing the incentive for players to chase points elsewhere after poor performances, while creating dedicated tournament-category weeks for a clearer structure.
The new ATP Masters 1000 tournament in Saudi Arabia will form part of that structure, with the ATP adding that players remained free to compete across the full breadth of the tour.
Players have become increasingly vocal about the physical toll of the season, arguing that the relentless schedule leaves too little time for recovery and increases the risk of fatigue and injury.
The rankings system has also come under scrutiny, with some players arguing that the pursuit of points can encourage them to keep competing even at non-mandatory events, making it harder to carve out meaningful breaks during the season.
The ATP said it would review the long-term structure of its competition formats, including potential changes to its doubles draws, with any prize money reallocated expected to go towards singles qualifying and early-round payouts.
Earlier this year, doubles players reacted angrily to suggestions that the tour planned to reduce the size of draws at tournaments, with the ATP arguing that it was looking at ways to create a more sustainable long-term model for the format.
'MORE COHERENT FOR ALL'
Gaudenzi, 53, who in February was re-elected for a third term through 2028, said the ATP's proposals would help players plan their seasons better, reward performances at the biggest events and broaden support.
The Italian added that the ATP would continue developing the proposals with its player and tournament advisory councils and board, aiming to bring a final package forward at its year-end meetings in Turin.
"OneVision has already helped strengthen our tour and the sport of tennis," Gaudenzi said of his organisation's long-term strategic plan.
"The next phase is an opportunity to make the season more coherent for players and fans and to ensure that the growth of the sport creates opportunity across the tour.
"Our immediate focus is the ATP Tour, but the ambition reaches further: ensuring tennis wins the competition for the next generation of fans."

Source: Reuters

items.title: Swedish parliament votes against Social Democrats leader as PM, as expected
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Sweden's parliament on Thursday rejected Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson's bid to form a minority government, as widely expected, extending a period of uncertainty over who will become prime minister after last month's general election.
items.body:
Sweden's parliament on Thursday rejected Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson's bid to form a minority government, [USN:L6N45K0F0 TEXT:"as widely expected"], extending a [USN:L8N4590Y1 TEXT:"period of uncertainty"] over who will become prime minister after last month's general election.
Four centre-left opposition parties, which have all said they favour Andersson as prime minister, on September 13 [USN:L1N455016 TEXT:"won a majority"] of seats in Sweden's parliament, the Riksdag, but do not agree on who should be part of a new government.
The opposition in September won 176 seats to 173 for Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's right-wing bloc. Thursday's ballot was [USN:L6N45Z0LR TEXT:"the first"] of up to four votes before a new election must be called
"It's been clear to me since the election night that it will take some time and that several ballots would likely be necessary to appoint a prime minister," Andersson told reporters after the vote in parliament
Only the Social Democrats voted in favour of Andersson, while the other parties voted against
The parliament speaker is widely expected to next ask Kristersson of the Moderates -- the second-biggest party after the Social Democrats -- to have a go at forming a government
There is little indication so far that Kristersson would be able to secure a majority, and the task of government formation could thus revert to Andersson at a later time

items.summary:
Tom Balmforth　Edward Carron

[ロンドン １５日 ロイター] - ロシアが、高速で迎撃が困難な「ジェット推進型」ドローン（無人機）の発射拠点をわずか６週間でほぼ完成させたことが、防衛専門家への取材や衛星画像の分析で分かった。ロシアはこの高速ドローンをウクライナへの攻撃に投入し、ウクライナは迎撃に苦戦している。

items.body:
Tom Balmforth　Edward Carron

[ロンドン １５日 ロイター] - ロシアが、高速で迎撃が困難な「ジェット推進型」ドローン（無人機）の発射拠点をわずか６週間でほぼ完成させたことが、防衛専門家への取材や衛星画像の分析で分かった。ロシアはこの高速ドローンをウクライナへの攻撃に投入し、ウクライナは迎撃に苦戦している。

ロシアはウクライナへの無人機攻撃に少なくとも１１カ所の固定発射拠点を使っており、今回の施設はそこに新たに加わる。場所はロシア南西部のロストフ州。 プラネット・ラボとエアバスが提供した商業衛星画像によれば、８月３１日時点では何もない原野だったが、１０月１４日までに、サッカー場約１２６面分の広さの複合施設に変わっていた。 約３．５キロメートルの場所にはミレロボ空軍基地がある。

建設期間は、ジェット推進型ドローンを使ったウクライナに対する攻撃が急増した時期と重なる。軍事アナリストは、ロシアが無人機の生産をジェット推進型にシフトしていると指摘する。

ジェット推進型ドローンは最高時速６００キロに達する。ウクライナ軍のデータによると、ロシアは夏の３カ月間でこの無人機の使用を約６倍に増やした。最も激しく攻撃されたのはキーウとその周辺地域だった。ウクライナが開発した迎撃用無人機は、旧型無人機を念頭にしたもので太刀打ちできない。ウクライナ政府は今、対策を急いでいる。

民間情報会社ドローンセックの創業者で最高経営責任者（ＣＥＯ）のマイク・モニク氏によると、施設の西端に最新型のジェット推進型ドローン「ゲラン４」と「ゲラン５」を発射できるレールを置くための台が８基ある。施設は完成が非常に近いように見え、「完全に稼働するまでにはおそらく数週間、もっと早い可能性もある」と述べた。 ロイターの分析では、８基の発射台のうち２基には既にレールが設置され、ほかの２基でもレールの設置が進んでいた。

ドローンセックは、新しい発射拠点は、ミレロボ空軍基地の防空システムの防御範囲（バブル）内とみられ、ウクライナがこの施設を攻撃するのは困難との見方を示した。

items.title: UK comedian Russell Brand's accuser told police she blamed herself for alleged rape
items.author: Sam Tobin
items.creator: Sam Tobin
items.summary: One of six women who allege British actor and comedian Russell Brand sexually assaulted them over a decade broke down in tears as she told police she blamed herself for being raped by him more than 25 years ago, his trial heard on Thursday.
items.body:
One of six women who allege British actor and comedian Russell Brand sexually assaulted them over a decade broke down in tears as she told police she blamed herself for being raped by him more than 25 years ago, his trial heard on Thursday.
Brand, once one of Britain's most high-profile broadcasters and the former husband of US singer Katy Perry, is on trial accused of three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault between 1999 and 2009.
The 51-year-old denies the allegations and told police after his arrest that he had never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity.
Prosecutors on Wednesday described him as being a ruthless sexual predator as his career progressed from stand-up comedy gigs to becoming a TV presenter and later a Hollywood movie star.
On the second day of his trial at London's Southwark Crown Court, jurors were played a police interview with a woman who says she met Brand at an event at the Labour Party conference in 1999, before he raped her in her hotel room.
"He knew what he was doing... he wanted to have sex that night and I was there," the woman said.
"I just remember him pushing me and I said 'no', but I was really scared ... I can't remember much after that."
She said a 2023 documentary, which made allegations of sexual misconduct against Brand, prompted her to contact police, adding: "I saw how manipulative he was ... I was thinking this is what he did to me but in a different way."
The woman also said: "I know I said 'no' ... I knew I couldn't get out of the situation. 'Do I shout, do I scream?'"
She told police that she felt that "this is something dirty that happened to me ... and I thought it was my fault", adding: "But in those days it was your fault, you know?"
The woman also said Brand had been "almost like trying to convince me it was all OK". She described it as "what abusers do".
Brand told her afterwards "don't worry, I get tested regularly", she added, and wrote his email address down for her.
'VORACIOUS' DESIRE Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones [USN:L8N4600OQ TEXT:"said on Wednesday"] that Brand's "strong desire for some form of sexual contact was indiscriminate and voracious".
Brand is alleged to have tried to drag a woman into a toilet cubicle at MTV Europe where she worked in 2001 and separately to have orally raped a woman in a toilet cubicle in a bar in 2004.
He is also charged with indecently assaulting a woman in 2004 or 2005, anally raping a fifth complainant after they had consensual sex at his home in 2009, and later that same year sexually assaulting a woman who worked for Channel 4.
All six complainants, who are legally entitled to lifelong anonymity, came forward after the 2023 documentary, Judge Joel Bennathan told jurors on Thursday.
He said the women whose allegations were featured in the documentary were not part of the trial and their accusations had not been tested in court.
He added: "The defence may suggest the programme caused the complainants, or at least some of them, to revisit historic sexual events and in their memories twist them from the consensual acts they were to the crimes they now allege."
The trial is expected to last around six weeks.

items.title: ＡＩで金融システミックリスク、ベアメタル復旧必要＝英中銀副総裁
items.author: ロイター
items.creator: ロイター
items.summary:
Rae Wee　Phoebe Seers

[バンコク／ロンドン １５日 ロイター] -
items.body:
Rae Wee　Phoebe Seers

[バンコク／ロンドン １５日 ロイター] - イングランド銀行（英中央銀行）のブリーデン副総裁は１５日、深刻なサイバー攻撃を受けた場合の復旧策について、銀行と協力して検討していると明らかにした。

同氏は人工知能（ＡＩ）を使ったサイバー攻撃を防御できると想定することはできないと指摘、ＡＩの進歩は世界の金融インフラに「システミックリスク」をもたらす水準に達したと警告した。

バンコクで開かれた国際金融協会（ＩＩＦ）の年次総会で「サイバー攻撃による侵入を防げると想定するだけでは十分ではない。中核サービスに必要な『ベアメタル復旧』の選択肢を検討する必要がある。金融システム全体を通じて、これを考えなければならない」と述べた。

いわゆる「ベアメタル」システムは、銀行の主要な技術基盤から完全に独立しており、主要システムが侵害された場合に稼働できる。

items.title: Prince Harry and wife Meghan make first joint appearance since UK return
items.author: Hannah McKay, Vitalii Yalahuzian
items.creator: Hannah McKay, Vitalii Yalahuzian
items.summary: Prince Harry and his wife Meghan appeared together in public on Thursday for the first time since they made a surprise return to Britain, returning to the city where they made their maiden joint official engagement nine years ago.
items.body:
Prince Harry and his wife Meghan appeared together in public on Thursday for the first time since they made a [USN:L8N44N0XA TEXT:"surprise return to Britain"], returning to the city where they made their maiden joint official engagement nine years ago.
Harry, the younger son of King Charles, and Meghan shocked the monarch and other members of the royal family when they relocated from California to England two months ago with their children Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5.
In their first joint public outing since then, the couple returned to Nottingham in central England which they visited in 2017, shortly after it was announced they were getting married.
They began by visiting a recording studio run by a youth and community charity which has received support from a [USN:L5N3UW0YL TEXT:"£1.1 million ($1.46 million) donation"] announced by Harry last year.
Later they were to visit a charity which tackles food poverty run by a group called Himmah to which Meghan donated £10,000 from sales of a cookbook released to raise funds in the wake of London's Grenfell Tower fire disaster.
The engagements conclude with a visit to another charity the couple have backed which supports young people and is linked to their previous visit in 2017.
HARRY AND MEGHAN DIVIDE PUBLIC OPINION Harry and Meghan, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, have become deeply polarising figures since they stepped down from royal duties to move to California in 2020, going on to deliver scathing criticism of both the prince's family and the royal institution itself.
Opinion polls show a majority of Britons hold a negative opinion of them, although young people are far more sympathetic.
On their visit to Nottingham nine years ago they were met by large flag-waving cheering crowds. Thursday's visit was a much lower-key affair, but the couple chatted with about 100 excited schoolchildren and well-wishers joined by large numbers of media.
Meghan looked emotional as one woman handed her a large bouquet of flowers and gave her a hug.
"We just wanted to support you," another well-wisher told her. "We wanted to be here ... we understand, we wanted you to know that we've shown you so much love."
When Harry made [USN:L1N4590X0 TEXT:"his first solo public appearance"] since their relocation he declared it was "good to be back on British soil" but their return has not been without difficulties.
The location of their new home has been kept private amid security concerns and they are not living in a royal residence.
They had to [USN:L8N45M0NT TEXT:"move their children"] to a new school not long after they started term because of concerns about security, with the couple's spokesperson also condemning the actions of "certain European paparazzi" intruding into their privacy.
($1 = 0.7549 pounds)

items.title: Client satisfaction scores rise slightly among banks, according to J.D. Power survey
items.author: The Canadian Press
items.summary: Canadians are slightly upping their customer satisfaction rankings for banks this year, according to a new J.D. Power survey, which says the higher scores are mainly driven by improvements in the Big ...
items.body: Canadians are slightly upping their customer satisfaction rankings for banks this year, according to a new J.D. Power survey, which says the higher scores are mainly driven by improvements in the Big Five banks. The survey showed that overall customer satisfaction rose by three points on a 1,000-point scale. RBC ranked the highest in terms of customer satisfaction among the Big Five banks for a third consecutive year, with a score of 619. BMO and CIBC were tied for second place, with a score of 611. TD Bank came in fourth with a score of 610. Among midsize banks, Tangerine Bank was ranked the highest for a 15th consecutive year with a score of 676. The survey points to a growing threat of competition, with newer fintechs outperforming Big Five lenders and midsize banks across certain key factors. The survey found 17 per cent of gen Z and gen Y traditional banking customers say they are likely or will definitely switch their primary lender in the next 12 months, which marked the highest level recorded in the past five years. Among younger customers, fees and competitive rates were found to be a vulnerability for larger banks. “Younger customers can be satisfied with their bank and still leave if they see a better opportunity to save money elsewhere,” Paul McAdam, senior director of banking and payments intelligence at JD Power, said in a news release. “When household budgets are tight, a monthly banking fee becomes an expense worth reconsidering. Traditional banks cannot take the next generation’s loyalty for granted.” The use of AI among lenders was seen to be unclear to most customers, with only 12 per cent of traditional retail bank customers indicating they understand how their lender uses AI. Meanwhile, fraud prevention and data security led the list in how customers prefer their bank to use AI. Survey results were taken from responses from 14,038 retail banking customers across large and mid-sized lenders. Responses were taken between January and February as well as from July to August. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026. Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press

BENGALURU, Oct 15 : Wipro, India's fourth-largest IT company, reported higher-than-expected second-quarter revenue on Thursday, helped by a revival in spending by its European clients and artificial intelligence unlocking new revenue streams.
The company's consolidated revenue rose 9.1 per cent to 247.53 billion rupees ($2.60 billion) in the July-September quarter, a tad above analysts' average estimate of 246.27 billion rupees, as per LSEG data.
Bengaluru-based Wipro forecast third-quarter revenue of $2.57 billion to $2.63 billion- which translates to a drop of 1.5 per cent to an increase of 0.5 per cent. Most brokerages had expected a guidance between 2 per cent decline and flat revenue growth.
Wipro said revenue from Europe, which contributes more than a fourth of its overall business, rose 5.1 per cent year-over-year, after stripping out currency fluctuations. The company also signed partnerships with Anthropic and Google during the year, helping it gain traction in terms of AI-related revenue and savings.

The company posted a net profit of 32.01 billion rupees, compared with analysts' estimates of 33.69 billion rupees.
Total deal wins for Wipro fell to $2.6 billion from $4.7 billion a year earlier. It inked pacts with industrial giant ABB, cybersecurity firm Crowdstrike and oil major Aramco during the quarter ended September 30.
Larger rivals TCS and HCLTech revenue figures were largely in-line with Street estimates but their stocks surged as investors welcomed the uptick in AI revenue. 
The company's Mumbai-listed shares closed 1.4 per cent higher ahead of the results, with the Nifty IT index rising 1.7 per cent.

Oct 15 : FC Midtjylland's UEFA Conference League opener at Albanian side KF Egnatia on Thursday has been moved from the Arena Kombetare in Tirana to the Elbasan Arena, the Danish club said.
UEFA changed the venue following discussions with local authorities in response to demonstrations in the capital.
Elbasan is about a 40-minute drive southeast of Tirana. 
Student organisers said the protests were over conditions at universities, higher education costs, a lack of both financial support and employment prospects after graduation.
The unrest follows months of mostly peaceful demonstrations sparked by plans to build a luxury resort on Albania's southern coast backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, a project that has faced legal challenges.

items.title: Roumanie-Deux bateaux en feu en mer Noire, sept marins portés disparus
items.author: Reuters
items.creator: Reuters
items.summary: Des équipes de secours roumaines sont à la recherche de sept membres d'équipage d'un des deux chimiquiers qui ont pris feu jeudi à la limite des eaux territoriales de la Roumanie en mer Noire, incident qui coïncide avec la détection d'une présence de drones russes dans l'espace aérien roumain, ont dit les autorités du pays.
items.body:
Des équipes de secours roumaines sont à la recherche de sept membres d'équipage d'un des deux chimiquiers qui ont pris feu jeudi à la limite des eaux territoriales de la Roumanie en mer Noire, incident qui coïncide avec la détection d'une présence de drones russes dans l'espace aérien roumain, ont dit les autorités du pays.
Le président roumain Nicusor Dan a déclaré que deux navires avaient été touchés par les drones, refusant de préciser si ceux-ci étaient russes. "Deux drones aériens les ont frappés", a-t-il dit à des journalistes à Bruxelles, en marge d'un sommet de l'Union européenne.
"Il y aura une réaction de l'Etat roumain", a-t-il affirmé, ajoutant être dans l'attente d'informations supplémentaires.
Les deux navires étaient ancrés près de l'embouchure du canal de Sulina, un bras du Danube qui se verse dans le mer Noire, devenu une voie de navigation majeure pour l'Ukraine depuis que la Russie a attaqué ses ports de mer Noire.
L'un des navires se situait dans les eaux roumaines, l'autre juste à l'extérieur.
La mer Noire et ses ports sont le théâtre d'attaques de plus en plus fréquentes dans le cadre de la stratégie d'asphyxie économique de l'adversaire tentée aussi bien par la Russie que par l'Ukraine, plus de quatre ans et demi après le début de l'invasion russe à grande échelle de l'Ukraine.
Depuis le début du mois, cinq navires commerciaux ont ainsi été [USN:L8N45Z11F TEXT:"touchés"] en mer Noire, au large des côtes de la Roumanie et de la Bulgarie, faisant un total de 23 morts ou disparus parmi les marins.
À LA RECHERCHE DES MARINS DISPARUS Pour éviter ces attaques, l'Ukraine s'appuie de plus en plus sur ses ports fluviaux le long du Danube et sur des voies de navigation proches des côtes de la Bulgarie et de la Roumanie, deux pays membres de l'Union européenne et de l'Otan.
Les autorités navales roumaines ont déclaré jeudi avoir reçu une alerte d'urgence provenant du chimiquier Wine Trader, battant pavillon de Saint-Marin, dont cinq des 12 membres d'équipage sont sains et saufs.
Mercredi soir, un navire transportant des produits chimiques et pétroliers, battant pavillon comorien, a également pris feu et l'équipage, sain et sauf, a dû être évacué.
Le ministère de l'Intérieur roumain a précisé avoir dépêché deux hélicoptères Black Hawk pour participer à la mission de recherche et de sauvetage, ainsi que deux navires avec du personnel médical à bord.
"Pour l'instant, les opérations de sauvetage ne peuvent pas être menées en toute sécurité en raison de très hautes vagues", a-t-il ajouté dans le communiqué.
La Roumanie partage une frontière de 614 km avec l'Ukraine, dont une grande partie longe le Danube. Elle a signalé des violations répétées de son espace aérien par des drones russes au cours des quatre dernières années.
Lors de son arrivée au sommet européen qui se tient ce jeudi et vendredi à Bruxelles, le Premier ministre bulgare Roumen Radev a déclaré qu'un projet de moratoire sur les attaques de navires civils en mer Noire était au menu des discussions.
"Aujourd'hui, nous allons discuter du moratoire proposé visant à mettre fin aux attaques contre les navires civils en mer Noire", a-t-il dit aux journalistes.

items.title: What is Starshield, Starlink's ‘military-grade’ version? How Ukraine uses two SpaceX systems against Russia | Explained
items.author: Akriti Anand
items.summary: SpaceX's Starlink is used for satellite-based communications, ground forces, logistics and defensive drones — ones that shoot down incoming drones. Meanwhile, Starshield is used for offensive military purposes.
items.body: SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield services, crucial to Ukraine's fight against Russia, were abruptly restricted on Tuesday night, Ukrainian officials alleged, according to an Axios report. The system turned off, they claimed, when a drone exceeded 160 kph. In some cases, it disconnected when the speed went over 80 kph.Ukraine relies on two satellite systems, Starlink and Starshield. Both systems were restricted, hampering drone strike missions and air defences, Ukrainian officials alleged, according to Axios.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said at a meeting in London with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, “We had massive [Russian] attacks today and it's a pity that we also had difficulties ... about Starlink and about intelligence and a lot of different surprises.”Meanwhile, a former Ukrainian minister commented on Starshield’s speed limit and posted on X, "Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h is being restored. Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defense."Ukraine's complaint drew renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink, SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, and Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon. While Musk has said the two systems are separate, in many cases, they share the same underlying satellite technology.Starlink and Starshield: What's the difference?SpaceX's Starlink is used for satellite-based communications, ground forces, logistics and defensive drones — ones that shoot down incoming drones. Meanwhile, Starshield is used for offensive military purposes.SpaceX boss Elon Musk did not directly comment on the alleged restrictions on Starlink and Starshield services, but he indirectly suggested which entity would be responsible for the limitations imposed on Ukraine.He posted on X, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."He also explained that "Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX".Musk said that the usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, "as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company".What is Starlink?Starlink, the main profit engine of SpaceX, is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper. Its roughly 13 million subscribers range from households and hikers to shipping companies and major airlines.The first Starlink satellites were launched in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets. Since then, the company has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers.SpaceX's Starlink gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how militaries operate on the battlefield.Starlink allows Ukraine to guide drones to Russian targets and also protect its own skies. It is not used for long-range Ukrainian missions that have successfully targeted Russian oil refineries in recent months.Musk has restricted Starlink for certain military uses while highlighting Starshield, a more secure network developed for government and military missions.What is Starshield?Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.While its missions are separate from Starlink's commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starlink cannot be used for offensive military action, SpaceX says. Starshield, however, allows those capabilities and uses enhanced encryption to transmit sensitive information.Starshield relies on the vast Starlink constellation as its backbone. It leverages the technology, engineering and operational experiences of Starlink, according to SpaceX.In addition, Starshield provides users with the ability to integrate sensors on objects like drones. The company says the militarised version can also provide users with Earth observation and the ability to integrate sensors or other payloads.As per SpaceX:1. Starshield launches satellites with sensing payloads and delivers processed data directly to the user.2. Starshield provides assured global communications to government users with Starshield user equipment.3. Starshield builds satellite buses to support the most demanding customer payload missions.Pentagon is the major buyerThe Pentagon, Starshield's largest customer, has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024.Questions over the relationship between Starlink and Starshield have persisted since Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022. SpaceX unveiled Starshield later that year, but the secrecy surrounding national security space programmes has left the precise boundaries between the two systems opaque.Those distinctions became a point of contention earlier this year when the Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over higher prices for satellite services used by military drones during the Iran conflict, Reuters reported.SpaceX argued that some customers paying roughly $5,000 per terminal for Starlink should instead have been using a Starshield service costing about $25,000 per terminal.Britain has also adopted Starshield. Under that arrangement, the service uses the same satellite constellation, ground stations and terrestrial infrastructure as Starlink, but operates through dedicated terminals and separate network gateways, Britain’s defence ministry has told Reuters.Other US partners are evaluating the system as well. New Zealand is doing a trial of Starshield to assess its usefulness for military operations, the New Zealand Defence Force previously told Reuters.(Inputs from Reuters)

items.title: Israeli firm used online ads to run vast spy operation, researchers say
items.author: Raphael Satter
items.creator: Raphael Satter
items.summary: Discover-Tech used a sprawling network of online ads to track targets and help hack their devices.
items.body:
Israeli digital advertising agency Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a sprawling network of online ads that it used to track targets and help hack their devices, two research groups said on Thursday.
Its services gave Israel's Candiru — a spyware company [USN:L1N2RU186 TEXT:"blacklisted by the US government"] — as well as other Israeli surveillance firms access to advertising platforms run by Google (GOOGL.O) , Comcast (CMCSA.O) , Russia's Yandex and others, according to separate reports from Canadian cyber watchdog group Citizen Lab and New York advertising security firm Confiant.
The reports show how the online advertising business, long a subject of privacy concerns, can also serve as a channel for sweeping espionage campaigns.
"The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat," Wolfie Cristl, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab, told Reuters. "For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike."
Discover-Tech's online ads — often for ordinary products such as phones or earpods — reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said.
Users who visited sites or used apps with the malicious ads could be identified and tracked by Discover-Tech, which would sometimes also try to extract phone numbers from some smartphone users, the researchers said. Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur.
Some ads would be used to help plant spyware from Candiru on users' devices, both research groups said, though Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a tiny fraction of Discover-Tech's overall volume.
MALICIOUS ADS SHOWN IN HUNDREDS OF SENSITIVE NETWORKS Confiant cofounder Jerome Dangu said Discover-Tech was pumping out at least 10 million ads per day all around the world and that data-sharing arrangements — called cookie matching — allowed it to track people even beyond the reach of its advertisements.
"Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said.
Discover-Tech, which was founded in 2020, did not return messages left via its contact form. A LinkedIn message and emails sent to its chief executive, Dekel Boni, were not returned.
Reuters' attempts to reach Candiru's owners were not successful. The US Commerce Department blacklisted Candiru in 2021 for [USN:L1N2RU186 TEXT:"allegedly supplying spyware"] that was used to maliciously target government officials, journalists, activists and academics.
Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech's ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025, something it said it was able to confirm because the media group had shared its network logs with the group. Al Jazeera did not return messages seeking comment.
Dangu of Confiant said that the malicious ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. He also said that some regions, like the Palestinian territories, were particularly saturated by the Israeli firm's ads.
"You go to almost any site in Palestine — any site — you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country," he said.
Citizen Lab also said it had similar evidence showing the malicious ads were shown to people in the United Nations, NATO, the European Commission, and more than a dozen other national governments. Other networks the ads appeared in included chip-related firms such as Nvidia (NVDA.O) , Sandisk (SNDK.O) , Broadcom (AVGO.O) , and Micron (MU.O) , as well as several media organizations in Mexico, Israel, and Europe that were not identified.
In addition to identifying Candiru and a couple of other surveillance vendors, Citizen Lab said it was able to glean some details about where Discover-Tech's users might be based because the firm inadvertently exposed its authentication logs to the internet, showing people logging in from internet protocol addresses in Israel, Europe, and the Gulf.
MEASURES AGAINST DISCOVER-TECH TAKEN Discover-Tech is now being frozen out of parts of the online ad market.
Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant's investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms "for systematically violating our policies."
IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an email that Discover-Tech had been suspended from its list of globally approved vendors last week after an audit identified policy violations.
Comcast ad tech subsidiary Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its platform "following recent activity," Comcast said in a statement. Yandex did not return Reuters messages seeking comment.
Advertising-driven surveillance is increasingly being seen as a national security threat. Earlier this year, the Pentagon said it had received reports that US forces deployed to war zones had been [USN:L6N4240BC TEXT:"targeted using location data"] harvested by ad tech firms and data brokers. Branches of the military have since [USN:L6N44V02G TEXT:"disabled ad tracking"] on some devices.

items.author: ロイター
items.creator: ロイター
items.summary: ［ブカレスト　１５日　ロイター］ -
items.body:
［ブカレスト　１５日　ロイター］ - ルーマニア当局は１５日、黒海の同国領海内で炎上した化学品タンカーについて、救助隊が行方不明の乗組員７人を捜索していると発表した。

火災に先立ち、ロシアの無人機（ドローン）がルーマニア領空に侵入していた。ルーマニア当局は、船舶火災とロシアの無人機との関連を明言していない。

前日夜に火災が起きた２隻のタンカーはともに、黒海からドナウ川へ通じる運河の河口付近に停泊していた。ロシアがウクライナの黒海沿岸の港を爆撃しているため、ウクライナはドナウ川の港や、ブルガリアとルーマニアの沿岸に近い航路への依存を強めている。

ルーマニアの海事当局は、サンマリノ船籍のタンカー「ワイン・トレーダー」から緊急通報を受けたと明らかにした。乗組員１２人のうち５人が救助され、７人が行方不明となっている。

内務省は捜索・救助活動にブラックホーク・ヘリコプター２機と、医療スタッフを乗せた船舶２隻を派遣したと発表した。声明で「波が非常に高く、現時点では安全に救助活動を行えない」と説明した。

コモロ船籍の化学品・石油タンカー「ヤラＪ」でも火災が発生したが、乗組員は全員無事だった。ルーマニア当局は当初、攻撃を受けたかどうかは不明としていた。

ここ数カ月、ロシアとウクライナの戦争に関連した黒海での船舶攻撃が増加し、世界的な食料危機を招く恐れが出ている。ブルガリアのラデフ首相は、欧州連合（ＥＵ）首脳が１５日、黒海での民間船舶への攻撃を一時停止する案を協議すると述べた。

items.title: Seven subpoenas engulf Nevada election chief in key midterm battle
items.author: Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff
items.creator: Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff
items.summary: As the Trump administration escalates its efforts to compel states to hand over voter rolls in search of fraud, the federal pressure is shaping a high-stakes rematch for Cisco Aguilar's job in Nevada, a top electoral battleground.
items.body:
The first Justice Department subpoena demanding voter information caught Democratic Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar off guard. It was June, and his office had been working informally with the FBI on routine [USN:L1N3XI0J6 TEXT:"election security"].
Weeks later, in a July 16 address from the Oval Office, President Donald Trump claimed without evidence that hundreds of thousands of noncitizens had registered to vote, citing an administration review. That review cited Nevada - a key prize in November's fight for control of the US Congress - as one of four states where noncitizen voter registration was widespread.
“We're going to be the target of this," Aguilar recalled telling Republican Governor Joe Lombardo before Trump’s address.
Then three more subpoenas seeking voter data arrived on September 1 and 2.
In total, the Justice Department would deliver seven subpoenas to Aguilar’s office between June 16 and September 2, a public records request shows.
As the Trump administration [USN:L6N45D0T4 TEXT:"escalates its efforts to compel states to hand over voter rolls "]in search of fraud, the federal pressure is shaping a high-stakes rematch for Aguilar's job in Nevada, a top electoral battleground.
As secretary of state, Aguilar is Nevada's chief election officer, responsible for overseeing elections and certifying results among other administrative duties.
The subpoenas have buried Aguilar in paperwork, distracting him from his own reelection campaign against Republican Jim Marchant, who falsely claims the 2020 election was rigged to favor Democrats and [USN:O8N31I01I TEXT:"whom Aguilar narrowly beat in 2022"].
Lombardo has not endorsed either candidate, and did not respond to a request for comment on whom he's supporting.
Trump has framed many of his election-related moves as an effort to help Republicans win seats in a year in which his party is widely expected to lose control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate. He has claimed without evidence that Democrats want noncitizens to be able to vote because their support would return them to power, a charge rejected by Democrats.
More than 50 election officials and election-law experts see multiple ways the Trump administration could potentially interfere with the 2026 midterms , Reuters reported on Wednesday. They identified potential flashpoints ranging from election-fraud claims and pressure on state officials to seizures of election materials and immigration enforcement near polling sites.
The White House says the administration's goal is to safeguard election integrity and voting security.
AGUILAR KEPT BUSY ANSWERING SUBPOENAS Aguilar said he considers the flood of subpoenas a deliberate attempt by the Trump administration to weaken his reelection bid and influence who will oversee Nevada's ballots in the 2028 presidential election.
A Justice Department spokesperson said the agency does not confirm or comment on grand jury subpoenas and declined to address Aguilar's assertions about political motivation. The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
Aguilar said his days were consumed by reassuring worried staff, pushing back on Trump's claims in media appearances, meetings with his personal lawyers and answering the subpoenas. Some donors had withdrawn support because they worried that support could harm their businesses, and his time for fundraising calls has dropped from as many as three hours a day to one a week, he said.
“If they can take me out in ‘26, they have control in ‘28,” said Aguilar, one of only two Democratic incumbent secretaries of state running in battleground states this cycle. “It’s absolutely intentional,” he told Reuters in an interview.
No other Democratic secretary of state - including in Arizona, the other battleground state where the incumbent is up for reelection - is known to have received any subpoenas, according to the Democratic Association of Secretaries of State and other secretaries in key swing states.
Unlike in states like Arizona where counties have more power, Nevada's elections process gives the secretary of state more control in administering elections, Aguilar and other secretaries of state said.
NO EVIDENCE OF WIDESPREAD VOTER FRAUD Marchant welcomed the federal spotlight, arguing it would lead voters to question Aguilar's stewardship.
"People are so tired of not trusting their election system," Marchant said in an interview, claiming without evidence that Aguilar has overseen elections rife with fraud.
Aguilar dismisses such assertions.
He pointed out that it was already illegal for noncitizens to vote in Nevada, as is true in all states for federal and state elections. His office had also investigated Trump's claims and has not found evidence that any of the people flagged by his administration were noncitizens, he said.
Nevada, whose voter base is roughly 30% Latino, narrowly swung toward Trump in 2024 by 46,000 votes.
Louis Jacobson, a senior columnist with the politics website Sabato’s Crystal Ball, moved the race toward Aguilar in September, writing that Marchant's election denialism likely won't be warmly received in a Democratic-friendly political environment.
Still, Jacobson told Reuters the Justice Department's focus could cause some voters to stay away from Aguilar if they think he's administered fraudulent elections. It could also elevate him as a defender against Washington overreach.
TRUMP'S PRESSURE CAMPAIGN The Trump administration has intensified a campaign to exert control over state elections, even as it struggles in court. The Justice Department has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia to provide voter data and has lost 26 of those cases, including against Nevada.
The Department of Homeland Security has claimed as many as 16,000 noncitizens are on Nevada's rolls, an effort Aguilar says is designed to intimidate Latino voters who may worry federal immigration agents could seek to detain them at polls.
In meetings, DHS officials told Nevada election officials it had thus far confirmed only 185 such cases, according to emails and a video seen by Reuters. Nevada officials, however, said in the emails their records indicated all 185 were citizens and that DHS had provided nothing substantive to suggest otherwise.
A DHS spokesperson said officials have since found that at least 2,000 names on the initial list of 16,000 were those of noncitizens. DHS said it had given Nevada enough information to parse the list on their own, but Aguilar said the agency had not yet provided the state with credible evidence.
Aguilar said the accusations were meant to exhaust his office and erode public trust.
"This whole series of events is like lasagna," he said. "You keep adding on layers of threats and pulling our resources to respond."
THE PRICE OF DEFIANCE The pressure has followed Aguilar home and across the state. Publicly, he has tried to project optimism and calm.
Aguilar recalled when he served as general counsel to tennis great Andre Agassi's business interests. Agassi had coaches and advisers around him, he said, but when a match began, he alone stepped onto the court.
Aguilar said he does not feel as isolated as Agassi did on those occasions, but as Nevada's top election official, he is the final decision-maker and the public face of the state's election system.
His initial concern about the subpoenas has now turned into defiance.
"Bring it," he said. They "don’t scare me."

LONDON, Oct 15 : AstraZeneca has teamed up with artificial intelligence biotech company insitro to discover and develop new treatments for difficult to treat liver and heart conditions, the British drugmaker said on Thursday.
Under the agreement, AstraZeneca will pay $40 million up front, with California-based insitro eligible for up to about $1.46 billion in potential development and commercial milestones, as well as a single-digit percentage of future sales in royalties.
The multi-year collaboration will focus on metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), a severe liver disease, and cardiomyopathies, a group of diseases that affect the heart muscle. Both have historically lacked effective therapies because researchers have struggled to pinpoint their root biological drivers, the drugmaker said.
Insitro will use its "Virtual Human" AI platform, which combines lab-grown cell models and machine learning, to identify causal disease biology and advance AstraZeneca-nominated targets from discovery to development-candidate stage. AstraZeneca will then run and fund future clinical trials.

The deal builds on insitro's expansion across the pharmaceuticals industry. The biotech company recently expanded its partnership with Bristol Myers Squibb to advance a broader portfolio of targets for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). It also teamed up with Eli Lilly to build AI models that predict pharmacological properties of small molecules in living organisms.
"Choosing the new targets that we want to put into our discovery pipeline is one of the hardest things we do across research and development," Sharon Barr, executive vice president of biopharmaceuticals R&D at AstraZeneca, told Reuters.
"By the time we read about a new pathway or target (in major scientific journals), it is no longer novel. It's in the public domain and we're already a few steps too late. But when we identify these unique connections early and test them in cellular systems, we're ahead of the game."
Barr added that pairing AI tools with experienced scientists allows the company to test fewer molecules in the lab, reduce guesswork and speed the search for effective medicines.

items.title: Warsh's quest for quiet Fed gets vocal pushback
items.author: Ann Saphir, Howard Schneider
items.creator: Ann Saphir, Howard Schneider
items.summary: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh’s call for a “quieter” central bank is facing pushback from colleagues who see public communication as a fundamental part of their job and have taken to TV, podcasts, interviews, social media and speakers' podiums to make their policy views known.
items.body:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh’s call for a “quieter” central bank is facing pushback from colleagues who see public communication as a fundamental part of their job and have taken to TV, podcasts, interviews, social media and speakers' podiums to make their policy views known.
Their voices have made a difference, with more than 40 appearances by nearly all of Warsh's colleagues at the central bank convincing traders to scale back rate-hike bets that had mounted after September's rate increase and Warsh's own silence on how much more the Fed may need to do.
Data on Wednesday showed consumer prices rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, shaking up financial markets' Fed expectations yet again. An October rate hike is now seen as a coin toss, an extraordinary lack of clarity that sharpens the focus on the stakes of Warsh's preference for silence.
Where the Warsh Fed's communications strategy will settle, however, remains an open question.
Warsh speaks in Bangkok on Friday at 0330 GMT (11:30 p.m. ET Thursday) at the International Monetary Fund's annual meeting, a final chance to shape market expectations for the Fed's decision in less than two weeks.
At every other opportunity, whether in talks to global central bankers in Sintra, Portugal, and Jackson Hole, Wyoming, or testimony before lawmakers, or answering questions from reporters at the Fed's headquarters, he has argued that the less Fed policymakers say about where they think rates should go, the more markets will be forced to take cues from economic data and make them a better source of information for the Fed as it makes its own rate decisions.
He has pared any hint of that so-called forward guidance from the Fed's post-meeting statement, and convened a task force widely expected to recommend jettisoning the rate-path projections produced quarterly that have been a staple of the Fed's communications for years.
Other policymakers, however, have been clear they will keep talking, in part because they think it is important for good monetary policy.
“If someone wants to present me with an argument that says, not speaking is going to help the public and households and businesses make better decisions and understand the economy, and it's going to help enhance our credibility as an institution, I'm all ears for it,” Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack told Reuters in an interview on Monday. "I think it's a pretty hard argument to make."
'MARKETS TOOK NOTE' Such a shift would mean upending decades of movement away from the cryptic style of Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, which Warsh openly admires. Indeed, US economists Robert Hall and Michael Woodford, whose pioneering research helped steer the Fed and other central banks toward more frank communications about the monetary policy outlook, this week were awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in economics.
Warsh's quiet Fed drive also comes as the Fed is trying to maintain and strengthen its accountability amid White House efforts to influence its monetary policy decisions and challenge its independence.
Uncharacteristically pointed remarks from New York Fed President John Williams and Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson were particularly effective in resetting rate-hike expectations.
"Markets took note of the fact that you had two members of the troika giving a very consistent message," said Richard Clarida, global economic advisor at investment firm PIMCO. The New York Fed chief and the Fed vice chair along with the Fed chair are typically the three most influential policymakers.
A former Fed vice chair himself, Clarida said he saw his role back then as communicating the chair's thinking, though he said he could not speak for whether that was still true today. "We're in a regime -- in a world -- where it's important to listen to all of the members of the committee," he said.
Speaking in Turkey last week, Fed Governor Christopher Waller gave his own assessment of what will be needed: "additional rate hikes...(that) do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."
Promising an exact rate path would keep the Fed from adjusting as needed to fresh information, Waller said, a risk Warsh has also raised.
But giving no signal at all, Waller said, "could surprise markets and create volatility," with investors pricing in a rate hike path that potentially exerts too little or far more restraint on the economy than what Fed policymakers see as necessary.
That appeared to have been the backdrop in recent weeks when Williams and Jefferson made the public case against rushing on rate hikes. Markets were expressing a strong conviction for a series of rate hikes at odds with the Fed's September dot plot that showed policymakers expected a less aggressive path.
VALUE OF COMMUNICATION That may also have been the situation in August, when markets bet heavily against a near-term rate hike after Warsh declined to offer a detailed rationale for July's decision to hold rates steady despite what he said was a "no tolerance" policy on inflation.
That time it was Warsh himself who broke the silence. Even as he repeated his call for a "quieter Fed," he said he wasn't convinced a recent cooling in inflation marked a clear trend -- a signal to markets a rate hike was, indeed, coming.
"Transparency about how the central bank is attempting to achieve their objective is important," Charles Evans, a former Chicago Fed president who championed a very strong form of forward guidance to help bolster the economy in the wake of the 2007-2009 financial crisis, told economists in Cleveland earlier this week.
Juhi Dhawan, macro strategist for Wellington Management, noted that remarks from Jefferson and Williams may have allowed Warsh to "get his message across without making himself be the conduit for it."
"I'm willing to give him some time to find that ideal form of communication," Dhawan said. "I think the value of communication has become apparent, if anything, in the last few months, as the Fed has tried to shift its trajectory on its rate path."
